title: Describe biological processes in plant physiology

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and respiration
lessons.html:
How plants capture and use energy

Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is the process in which green plants use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into sugars, releasing oxygen:

6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + 6O₂

It takes place in chloroplasts, mainly in leaves, where the green pigment chlorophyll absorbs light. There are two stages: the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membranes, which split water, release oxygen and produce energy carriers (ATP and NADPH), and the Calvin cycle in the stroma, which uses these carriers to fix CO₂ into sugars.

C3, C4 and CAM plants

TypeExamplesFeatures
C3Wheat, soybeans, potatoes, most treesEfficient in cool, moderate conditions; lose efficiency in heat through photorespiration
C4Maize, sugarcane, sorghum, many summer veld grassesConcentrate CO₂, efficient in heat and high light, better water use
CAMPineapple, agave, many succulentsOpen stomata at night, very water efficient

Factors limiting photosynthesis

Light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature, water supply and nutrients (especially nitrogen and magnesium for chlorophyll). The factor in shortest supply limits the rate. Farm practices such as plant spacing, canopy management, irrigation and fertilisation aim to remove limitations.

Respiration

Respiration breaks down sugars to release energy for growth and maintenance, using oxygen and producing CO₂ and water. It occurs day and night in all living cells, including roots and stored produce. Roots in waterlogged soil cannot respire properly due to lack of oxygen. After harvest, fruit and vegetables keep respiring, using up sugars and producing heat; cooling slows respiration and extends shelf life.

lessons.title: Water, nutrients and transport
lessons.html:
Moving water and food through the plant

Water uptake and transpiration

Water enters roots mainly through root hairs by osmosis, moves up through the xylem and evaporates from leaves through stomata (transpiration). Transpiration pulls water up in a continuous column, cools the leaf and carries dissolved minerals. Stomata open to take in CO₂ but lose water at the same time, so plants balance carbon gain against water loss. In drought, stomata close, photosynthesis slows and growth drops.

Osmosis and salinity

Osmosis is the movement of water across a membrane from a lower to a higher solute concentration. If the soil solution is very salty, water moves less easily into roots, and plants show drought-like stress even in wet soil. This is why salinity is a serious problem on some irrigated lands.

Mineral nutrition

NutrientMain roleTypical deficiency sign
Nitrogen (N)Proteins, chlorophyllYellowing of older leaves
Phosphorus (P)Energy transfer, roots, floweringPurplish leaves, poor root growth
Potassium (K)Water regulation, qualityScorched leaf margins on older leaves
Calcium (Ca)Cell wallsDisorders in fruit, e.g. blossom-end rot in tomatoes
Magnesium (Mg)Chlorophyll centreYellowing between veins of older leaves

Mobile nutrients (N, P, K, Mg) move to young growth, so deficiency appears first on older leaves; immobile nutrients (Ca, B, Fe) show symptoms on young growth.

Phloem transport

Sugars made in leaves (sources) move through the phloem to sinks: growing shoots, roots, fruit and storage organs. Management practices like fruit thinning or girdling change this source-sink balance.

lessons.title: Growth, development and plant hormones
lessons.html:
How plants grow and respond

Growth and development

Growth is the increase in size through cell division and enlargement at meristems: apical meristems at shoot and root tips lengthen the plant; lateral meristems (cambium) thicken stems. Development refers to changes in stage: germination, vegetative growth, flowering, fruit set, ripening and senescence.

Germination

A seed needs water, a suitable temperature and oxygen (and for some species light or darkness) to germinate. Water activates enzymes that break down stored food to feed the embryo until the seedling can photosynthesise. Planting too deep, in cold or waterlogged soil reduces emergence.

Plant hormones

HormoneMain effects
AuxinsCell elongation, apical dominance, root formation on cuttings
GibberellinsStem elongation, germination, fruit growth
CytokininsCell division, delay of leaf ageing, bud growth
EthyleneFruit ripening, leaf and fruit drop
Abscisic acidStomatal closure in drought, dormancy

Responses to the environment

  • Photoperiodism: flowering controlled by day length; short-day, long-day and day-neutral plants. Onion bulbing, for example, depends on day length, so cultivars must suit the latitude.
  • Vernalisation: some plants need a cold period to flower, such as some winter cereals.
  • Dormancy and chilling: deciduous fruit trees need sufficient winter chill to break bud dormancy evenly; warm winters cause uneven budbreak.
  • Tropisms: growth towards light (phototropism) and in response to gravity (gravitropism).

Applying physiology

Understanding these processes helps explain why irrigation timing, fertilisation, pruning, cultivar choice and post-harvest cooling work.

Key points

  • Photosynthesis makes sugars from CO₂ and water using light; respiration releases energy from sugars.
  • C4 plants such as maize are efficient in heat; C3 plants such as wheat suit cooler conditions.
  • Water moves up the xylem; sugars move in the phloem from sources to sinks.
  • Deficiency of mobile nutrients shows first on older leaves.
  • Hormones and environmental signals control growth, flowering, ripening and dormancy.
